claims.text: Differences in elemental surface energy and atomic mobility cause selective segregation in high-entropy alloy nanoparticles under high-temperature thermoelectric conditions.
At 473–773 K, configurational entropy is sufficient to maintain a single-phase solid solution in the nanoparticles.
The initial nanoparticles contain five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and are crystallized as a single-phase solid solution.
Exposure at 1273–1923 K triggers phase segregation and/or formation of minor intermetallic or ordered phases.
The structural transition is triggered by temperature-dependent differential atomic diffusion.
Elements with lower surface energy preferentially segregate during thermal exposure.
Phase stability is governed by competition between configurational-entropy stabilization and an enthalpic preference for phase separation.
Differences in surface energies, atomic sizes, and mixing enthalpies mediate the enthalpic preference for phase separation.
Higher temperature increases atomic mobility and thereby permits structural reordering and phase separation.
At higher temperatures, the enthalpic contribution dominates over configurational-entropy stabilization.
After exposure at 473–773 K, the nanoparticles will retain their original single-phase solid-solution structure.
After exposure at 1273–1923 K, the nanoparticles will exhibit second phases, ordering, or compositional inhomogeneity.
XRD peak splitting or additional peaks can indicate the formation of secondary phases.
Spatially non-uniform EDX elemental maps can reveal chemical segregation.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes low-temperature stability to configurational entropy but states that enthalpy dominates at higher temperature. For a fixed system, the thermodynamic free-energy contribution from configurational entropy scales with temperature; the proposed high-temperature reversal therefore requires an additional explanation, such as low-temperature kinetic trapping or temperature-dependent phase entropies. Increased mobility can explain access to equilibrium but does not itself make the enthalpic term thermodynamically larger relative to TΔS.
